title: Infra Runbook: GPU Fleet & Capacity + CI/CD/IaC Practices
author: Ethan Zhao
content:
Summary
---
This runbook consolidates our recommended practices for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud accounts and networking configuration, Terraform/IaC modules, and CI/CD build pipelines used to manage the Redwood Inference serving infrastructure. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for provisioning, operating, and scaling inference clusters.

Goals
- Provide a single reference covering capacity targets, autoscaling behavior, and safety thresholds.
- Standardize IaC modules and CI/CD patterns to reduce variance between environments.
- Document operational runbooks and escalation paths for GPU capacity incidents.

Ownership and Applicability
- Primary owners: Infra / GPU Fleet team (eng-infra).
- Secondary owners: Eng SRE, Eng Platform, Security (networking/KMS).
- Applies to: Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment infra managed by Terraform in cloud accounts (AWS/GCP currently).

1) GPU Fleet & Capacity Planning
Overview
We operate heterogeneous GPU pools (A100-40GB, A100-80GB, H100) across regions. Capacity planning must balance latency SLOs, cost targets, and model memory requirements.

Targets and SLOs- 95th percentile token latency per request: <= 250ms (short prompts), <= 700ms (long prompts <= 4k tokens)
- Cluster CPU util target: 20-60% (to leave headroom for spikes)
- GPU utilization target by pool: 50-75% (sustained >80% triggers scale-up)
- Cold-start tail: < 1% of requests experience >2s cold start

Capacity Rules and Thresholds
1. Scale up when: average GPU utilization across pool > 65% for 10m OR request queue length > 50 for 5m.
2. Scale down when: average GPU utilization < 40% for 30m AND queue length < 10.
3. Emergency scale-up: if request queue > 500 sustained for 2m, trigger immediate burst nodes and notify oncall.

Capacity Calculation (example)- Baseline QPS per A100-80GB: 40 requests/s for small models; 8 requests/s for 70B models (varies by sequence length).
- Example: expected steady traffic 3,600 rps for small models -> required GPUs = ceil(3600 / 40) = 90 GPUs (add 20% buffer => 108 GPUs).

2) Cloud Accounts & Networking
Network Topology- VPC per region with standard subnets: public (for bastion/limited APIs), private (for runtime and management services), and tooling (CI/CD agents).
- Peering and Transit: Use VPC Peering or Transit Gateway for cross-account access. Inter-region peering must be restricted to telemetry/monitoring endpoints.

Security & Access- Bastion hosts enforced for interactive access; Session Manager preferred.

KMS keys per account and environment; HSM for customer-sensitive Private deployments.

Egress & Cost Controls
- Apply egress guardrails: deny wide-open outbound rules from runtime subnets; use NAT gateways with egress cost dashboards.

Connectivity checklist (table)
| Component | Required Config | Owner | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| VPC | cidr 10.<env>.<region>.0/20 | infra-networking | Documented in account template |
| Subnet tiers | public/private/tooling with route tables | infra-networking | private subnets for runtimes |
| Security groups | Open only necessary ports (22/443/1977) | infra-team | 1977 = runtime control plane |

3) Terraform / IaC Modules
Module Standards
- All modules must be documented in the infra module registry and support inputs for environment (dev/staging/prod), region, and sizing.
- Use semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Modules must include CHANGELOG.md.

Required Modules (examples)
- compute/gpu-pool: defines ASG/instance group, instance profile, AMI bootstrapping, GPU drivers, node labels.
- networking/vpc: VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT, IGW, flow logs.
- iam/roles: least-privilege roles for runtime, autoscaler, CI runners.
- monitoring/prometheus: scrape configs, exporters, node metrics.

Example: gpu-pool module inputs (YAML-like snippet)
```
module: compute/gpu-pool
inputs:
  env: prod
  region: us-west-2
  instance_type: p4d.24xlarge
  desired_count: 20
  min_count: 5
  max_count: 200
  autoscaler_policy:
    scale_up_cpu_threshold: 65
    scale_down_cpu_threshold: 40
```

Best Practices
- Keep bootstrapping scripts idempotent and small; bake AMIs for faster scale-up.
- Use SSM parameter store for config values and secrets reference.
- Validate modules with unit tests (terratest) and policy-as-code (OPA/Conftest).

4) CI/CD and Build Pipelines
Pipelines overview
- CI runs for IaC: plan -> validate -> unit tests -> merge gating.
- CD for infra: merge to main triggers gated apply in staging; manual approval for prod applies.

Pipeline requirements
- Terraform plan artifacts must be stored and reviewed before apply.
- Automatic drift detection weekly for critical modules.

Recommended Git workflow
1. Feature branch for module changes.
2. Open PR with terratest results and plan output.
3. Approval from module owner + infra security.
4. Merge triggers apply in staging.

CI checks (pre-merge)
- terraform fmt/check
- terraform validate
- terratest (unit)
- conftest (policy)

CD gating rules
- Staging: auto-approve applies on merge.
- Prod: require two approvals (module owner + infra oncall) and deploy window tag.

5) Operational Runbooks (incidents & recoveries)
Runbook: High GPU Queue / Scale Failure
1. Detect: Pager alert from autoscaler: "gpu-pool queue > 500" or "scale_up_failed".
2. Immediate actions:
  a. Confirm metric in Grafana (GPU queue length, request latency, cluster utilization).
  b. Check autoscaler logs (k8s HorizontalPodAutoscaler / cloud autoscaling events).
  c. If autoscaler failing due to quota, open cloud quota increase request and trigger emergency burst using reserved burst pool runbook.
3. If nodes failing to provision (AMI/driver issues):
  a. Roll back to previous AMI version by updating module input and manually triggering apply for the pool.
  b. Replace problematic launch template and force-replace affected instances.
4. Communication:
  a. Post to #oncall-status with incident summary and mitigation steps.
  b. If >15 minutes customer impact, escalate to Eng SRE lead and Customer Success.

Runbook: Networking / Control Plane Partition
1. Detect: telemetry gaps, control-plane 502/504 or agent heartbeats missing.
2. Actions:
  a. Confirm security group/route table changes in last 30m.
  b. Validate VPC connectivity: traceroute to control-plane endpoint from affected subnet.
  c. If caused by recent Terraform change, revert terraform apply for networking module and notify security.

6) Playbook: Day-2 Operations and Routine Tasks
Weekly
- Run drift detection for critical modules.
- Validate monitoring alerts thresholds and dashboards.

Monthly
- Review GPU capacity forecasts with product (growth + model onboarding).
- Review reserved instance commitments and cloud discounts.

Quarterly
- Load test on staging with representative prompt sets to validate autoscaling behavior.

7) Troubleshooting Tips & Commands
- View GPU pool autoscaler logs:
  kubectl -n infra logs deployment/autoscaler -f --since=1h
- Check GPU driver status on a node:
  nvidia-smi -L && nvidia-smi topo --matrix
- Re-run terraform plan for a module:
  cd infra/modules/compute/gpu-pool && terraform init && terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars
- Trigger a manual scale up (temporary):
  aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name gpu-prod-usw2 --desired-capacity 150 --honor-cooldown

8) Post-Incident: Regression & Change Controls
- Every capacity incident >30m must produce a short postmortem with timeline, root cause, mitigation, and follow-up actions.
- Follow-up actions must be tracked in Jira and assigned owners with ETA.

Appendix A: Module Naming & Example Repos
- infra/modules/compute/gpu-pool

Appendix B: FAQs
- Q: How do we handle region-specific GPU shortages?
  A: Route low-priority work to alternative region pools via smart routing policies; notify product for model routing changes.
